Collective Security. Collective security is the principle that an attack on one nation constitutes a threat to all, binding countries to defend each other through collective action rather than unilateral force or alliances. Developed after World War I as an alternative to the balance-of-power politics that produced imperial wars, it was enshrined in the League of Nations and later NATO. Though elegant in theory, collective security repeatedly failed, most catastrophically in the 1930s when aggressors exploited the League's lack of enforcement power. Collective security emerged from the Paris Peace Conference (1919) and the League of Nations Covenant (1920), intended to prevent future wars by making aggression illegitimate and requiring member nations to enforce peace collectively. The League's fundamental weakness was lack of enforcement: it had no standing army and member nations could opt out of military action; when Japan invaded Manchuria (1931) and Italy invaded Ethiopia (1935), the League imposed only ineffectual sanctions. Nazi Germany exploited this paralysis: the Munich Conference (1938) exemplified appeasement, where France and Britain sacrificed Czechoslovakia to Hitler without invoking collective security, hoping to avoid war rather than enforce the system. World War II discredited the League and prompted redesign of collective security in the United Nations Charter (1945), which created the Security Council with permanent members (veto power) and enforcement authority. NATO (1949) represented a regional variant of collective security against Soviet Union, binding North Atlantic democracies to common defense under Article 5: an attack on one is an attack on all. The concept remains aspirational: the United Nations lacks enforcement power; regional alliances succeed irregularly; major powers continue pursuing national interest over collective obligation.
